analysis.one_liner: Legalized unlocking cell phones and breaking digital locks for any lawful, non-infringing use.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: introduced in March 2015, it sat in the House Judiciary and Ways and Means Committees for the rest of the two-year Congress and expired.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed federal copyright law so that breaking a digital lock — on a phone, a movie, software, or any device — is only illegal when it actually infringes a copyright, rather than being illegal in itself. It also would have written into statute the right to unlock a cell phone you own so it works on another carrier, without the original carrier's blessing, and directed the President to adjust trade agreements that conflict with these rules. It never advanced past a House committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy cell phones and other electronic devices: they could unlock a phone they paid for to switch carriers, repair and modify their own devices, and make or sell tools that bypass digital locks for lawful purposes — without risking a lawsuit under copyright law. Small repair shops, resellers, and the used-phone market would also gain, since devices could legally be moved between networks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cell phone owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: It allows owners to unlock a phone they bought to switch to a new carrier without the original carrier's permission, provided the new network agrees to serve them.

It makes it legal to circumvent a digital lock, and to make or sell tools that do so, when the purpose is a lawful, non-infringing use — so consumers and small businesses would no longer risk lawsuits for legitimate uses of products they own.
It directs a Commerce Department report on how the digital-lock law affects consumer choice and competition, and whether it should be reformed or repealed.

analysis.who_pays: Wireless carriers would lose a tool for keeping customers tied to their networks, and entertainment and software companies would lose the sweeping legal protection that lets them punish anyone who breaks a digital lock even for a lawful use. Consumers would bear none of the cost directly, though opponents argued weaker lock protection could mean more piracy and less investment in digital content.

drawbacks.text: Critics of weakening section 1201 argue that allowing the manufacture and trafficking of tools that break digital locks whenever the maker claims a non-infringing purpose would make it harder to stop piracy, since infringement is judged after the fact and the tools are widely usable for copying.

The bill requires the President to renegotiate parts of existing trade agreements to match the new law, which could put the United States in conflict with trading partners and treaty commitments it had already accepted.
The protection for unlocking applies only where the owner has consent from or an agreement with the new network operator, so it would not help with every locked-device situation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real but modest: legal certainty for phone unlocking and removal of the threat of lawsuits against lawful, non-infringing uses. The costs are the ones critics would name: weakening the bright-line ban on trafficking in circumvention tools could make digital piracy harder to police, and rewriting trade commitments is slow and uncertain. On balance, the bill would have shifted control over devices consumers already own back to consumers, at a genuine but debatable cost to copyright enforcement. Its worst design flaw was procedural: instead of debating it, Congress let it die.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in March 2015 and to a Judiciary subcommittee a month later, and neither the committee nor the full House ever acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Zoe Lofgren introduced the bill on March 24, 2015, with Thomas Massie, Jared Polis, and Anna Eshoo as original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and, additionally, to the Ways and Means Committee the same day it was introduced.
On April 21, 2015, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet — the last recorded action.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate companion action is recorded in the bill's history before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wireless carriers and large copyright holders kept the status quo, in which digital locks stay enforceable regardless of whether breaking one infringes anyone's copyright.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wireless carriers and major copyright holders

for.name: Rep. Zoe Lofgren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was joined by three colleagues as original cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. Thomas Massie, Jared Polis, and Anna Eshoo
6 of 435 House Democrats and 1 of 246 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, for a total of 7 cosponsors — too few to move it in committee.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of primary jurisdiction (Chair: Rep. Bob Goodlatte, R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in March 2015 and sent it to its intellectual property subcommittee, then took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Wireless carrier industry
against.role: Major carriers and their trade association (CTIA)
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed restoring a statutory right to unlock phones, arguing carrier locking protects network security and subsidized handset financing.

against.name: Entertainment and software copyright industries
against.role: Motion picture, music, and software companies
against.what_they_did: Long opposed weakening section 1201's anti-circumvention ban, arguing it is essential protection against digital piracy.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but small — 6 Democrats and 1 Republican among 7 cosponsors — and the bill died in committee without a recorded vote, so no party position was ever tested on the floor.

industries.note: Carriers benefit from phones locked to their network, which helps keep customers from switching and lets them control resale and trade-in terms. The bill would end the legal basis for keeping a phone tied to the original carrier's network.

These companies use digital locks (DRM) to control how movies, music, games, and software are used and to shut down tools that break the locks. The bill would allow breaking locks for any non-infringing purpose, shrinking the leverage section 1201 gives them over consumers and independent creators.

industries.industry: Independent repair shops, resellers, and third-party unlocking services
industries.note: Making and selling unlocking tools or servicing a locked phone would be clearly legal again, restoring a small business market that the current law's trafficking ban suppresses.

industries.industry: Cell phone buyers and the secondary phone market
industries.note: Everyday buyers could take a paid-off phone to any compatible carrier and used phones would be worth more because they could work across networks.
